strengths: Addresses an important and timely question for the mechanistic interpretability community: whether interventions that produce off-distribution representations can still support valid causal claims about a model's natural mechanisms.
The harmless vs. pernicious taxonomy of divergence is a useful conceptual framing, and the paper is careful to note that divergence does not automatically invalidate interpretability claims.

The toy constructions in Section 4 (mean-difference patching activating a previously silent ReLU unit; dormant behavioral changes triggered by context-dependent pathways) are concrete, clearly worked examples that make the failure modes tangible, and the paper honestly acknowledges connections to prior work on off-manifold patching (Makelov et al. 2023, Zhang & Nanda 2024, counterfactual explanation literature).

The empirical survey in Section 3 (MDVP, SAEs, Boundless DAS on Llama-3-8B) with EMD-based quantification and baseline correction is a reasonable first step toward establishing that divergence is common rather than method-specific.

The writing is clear, the limitations are candidly discussed (e.g., admitting there is no reliable method to classify pernicious divergence and that the CL loss is not specific to pernicious cases), and the appendix provides enough detail for reproduction of the synthetic experiments.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core observation that off-manifold interventions can activate unrepresentative pathways and confound patching-based conclusions has been extensively discussed in prior work (Makelov et al. 2023, Wattenberg & Viégas 2024, Huang et al. 2024, adversarial/counterfactual-manifold literature). The main new elements are the taxonomy framing and a small modification of Grant (2025)'s CL loss (averaging over vector labels, restricting to causal subspaces), which is incremental.

The 'theoretical analysis' consists of hand-constructed two-layer ReLU examples with manually chosen weights rather than general theorems. The results are intuitive (off-manifold points can activate silent units; convex hull projection removes the effect) and their generality to realistic networks is not established.

The empirical Section 3 evidence is largely qualitative (2D PCA scatter plots) and uses small samples (100–2000 vectors); the EMD measurements with baseline correction do not demonstrate that any observed divergence actually changes a mechanistic conclusion in a real model. No case study shows a real interpretability claim being wrong because of divergence.

The proposed mitigation (adapted CL loss) is evaluated only on a synthetic MLP dataset with two causal dimensions plus Gaussian noise dimensions. There are no experiments on real language models, no comparison against existing manifold-constrained counterfactual methods (e.g., Verma et al. 2024), and the OOD improvement over the behavioral-only baseline appears modest and is not shown to prevent pernicious divergence specifically.

The paper cannot distinguish harmless from pernicious divergence in practice, which limits the actionable value of the taxonomy: the proposed loss reduces all divergence along causal dimensions, which the authors themselves note may be overly blunt and, per their own harmless-case analysis, could remove desirable, informative divergence.

Scope and significance: given the synthetic-only validation and toy theory, the practical impact on how interpretability experiments are conducted remains speculative; the significance rests mostly on raising awareness rather than delivering validated tools or results.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored question in mechanistic interpretability: whether interventions that produce off-distribution representations still support faithful claims about the model's natural mechanisms.
The taxonomy of 'harmless' vs. 'pernicious' divergence is a useful conceptual framing, and the paper is honest that the two categories are not mutually exclusive.
The related work section is thorough and carefully positions the contribution relative to prior critiques of activation patching (e.g., Makelov et al. 2023, Huang et al. 2024, Sutter et al. 2025).

The empirical demonstration in Section 3 that divergence is common across multiple intervention methods (mean-difference patching, SAE reconstruction, DAS) on a real LLM (Meta-Llama-3-8B) is a useful sanity check, and the EMD-based quantification with baseline correction is methodologically reasonable.
The limitations section is candid, acknowledging that no reliable method for classifying pernicious divergence is provided and that the proposed solution is preliminary.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is not actually theory in a meaningful sense: Sections 4.1 and 4.2 consist of hand-constructed 4-dimensional numerical examples rather than general theorems with conditions, proofs, or characterizations of when divergence is harmful. The 'general condition' in Section 4.2.1 is a one-line restatement of the example, and the dormant-behavior result in 4.2.2 is again a bespoke toy construction. It is unclear how these examples transfer to realistic networks.

The empirical evidence for the central 'pernicious divergence' phenomenon is entirely synthetic or illustrative. There is no demonstration that hidden-pathway activation or dormant behavioral changes actually occur in a real language model under standard intervention methods — only that representational divergence (Section 3) exists. The gap between 'distributions differ' and 'mechanistic conclusions are invalidated in practice' is never empirically closed.

The proposed mitigation (the adapted CL loss) is evaluated only on a tiny synthetic MLP dataset (10 classes, 66 dimensions) with DAS. There are no experiments on real models, so the practical utility of the method for the settings the paper criticizes (LLM interpretability) is unestablished. The authors themselves admit the method is 'broad-stroke' and 'not specific to pernicious divergence,' which substantially weakens contribution 4.

The novelty of the core observation is limited. That off-manifold interventions can activate atypical circuits and confound patching conclusions has been implicitly explored in prior work the paper itself cites (Wattenberg & Viégas 2024, Makelov et al. 2023, Zhang & Nanda 2024, Chen et al. 2025). The paper's main additions — the harmless/pernicious taxonomy and the CL-loss adaptation — are incremental over Grant (2025) and Makelov et al. (2023) respectively.

The empirical divergence study in Section 3 is narrow: one task, a handful of layers, cherry-picked or arbitrarily selected layers (e.g., 'layer 10 as it had the lowest EMD'), and reliance on qualitative 2D PCA visualizations whose relationship to functional consequences is unexamined. The paper concedes the EMD measure 'did not necessarily correlate with the subjective interpretation.'

The paper offers no actionable diagnostic. The recommendations in Section 4.2.2 (report newly active ReLUs, project onto manifolds, test context-sensitive flips) are stated but not evaluated — the manifold projection experiment is a single unverifiable sentence in the toy example.

Significance is questionable: the practical takeaway for practitioners is largely negative ('any divergence outside the null-space is potentially pernicious') with an immature mitigation restricted to synthetic settings. For a top-tier venue, the contribution reads as a position/discussion paper with limited technical depth and incomplete empirical support.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and key experimental details (e.g., how the 100 contexts for MDVP were sampled, SAE hyperparameters, DAS training details beyond learning rate) are deferred or underspecified.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question for mechanistic interpretability: whether causal interventions (activation patching, SAE reconstruction, DAS) push representations off the model's natural distribution, and what that means for the validity of mechanistic claims.

Provides a useful conceptual taxonomy distinguishing 'harmless' divergence (null-space variation, covariance within decision boundaries) from 'pernicious' divergence (activation of hidden pathways, dormant behavioral changes), which clarifies when divergence should worry practitioners.

The toy constructions in Section 4 (mean-difference patching activating a ReLU unit silent on natural inputs; dormant behavioral changes appearing only under specific context vectors) are concrete, verifiable, and effectively illustrate how behaviorally confirming intervention results can arise from off-manifold mechanisms rather than genuine circuitry.

Empirical Section 3 demonstrates that representational divergence arises across multiple method families (MDVP, SAE, DAS) on a real LLM (Llama-3-8B-Instruct), with reasonable quantification via baseline-corrected EMD.
Honest and substantive limitations discussion; the authors do not overclaim that their adapted CL loss is a final solution and note the absence of a reliable perniciousness classifier.
The paper is generally well written and clearly motivated, with good positioning against related work on interpretability illusions, causal scrubbing, and manifold-constrained counterfactuals.
weaknesses: Theoretical contribution consists of hand-constructed, illustrative examples on tiny two-layer ReLU networks rather than general theorems; the generality of the harmless/pernicious taxonomy beyond these curated settings is not established, and the 'general condition' is essentially a restatement of the example.

The proposed mitigation (adapted CL loss) is evaluated exclusively on a synthetic 2D-grid-plus-noise MLP task; there is no demonstration on a real network that the loss reduces pernicious divergence or improves the reliability of mechanistic conclusions, leaving the practical value of the method unvalidated.
The methodological novelty over Grant (2025) is incremental: averaging CL vector targets over all valid natural latents and restricting the loss to causal subspaces is a modest modification.

No empirical comparison against alternative manifold-constraining baselines (e.g., Verma et al., 2024, which the paper itself cites as directly constraining intervened features to the natural manifold).

Section 3's empirical findings are largely qualitative (PCA scatter plots over a small number of layers); the paper acknowledges that divergence alone does not show the studied methods are invalid, so the practical impact of the demonstrated EMD shifts on published mechanistic claims remains unclear.

The harmful/pernicious distinction is admitted to be claim-dependent and the paper offers no operational procedure for classifying which divergences are pernicious in practice, which limits the actionable value of the framework.

Scope is narrow overall: one model, a few layers, and one synthetic testbed for the solution; reproducibility details exist but key choices (e.g., layer selection based on lowest EMD) risk selection effects.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexamined question in mechanistic interpretability: whether standard causal interventions produce off-distribution representations and how this affects the faithfulness of resulting explanations

Combines theory, illustrative synthetic examples, and real-model experiments: a proposition showing coordinate patching guarantees divergence on most manifold geometries (with a clean characterization of patch-closed sets as Cartesian products/hyperrectangles in Appendix A.2), concrete hand-worked examples of 'harmless' null-space divergence and 'pernicious' hidden-pathway activation, and EMD-based quantification of divergence across three popular methods (mean-difference patching, SAEs, DAS) on a real LLM
The harmless-vs-pernicious taxonomy, including dormant behavioral changes that alter behavior in other contexts, is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution for interpreting patching results

Proposes a practical mitigation by adapting the Counterfactual Latent (CL) loss to Boundless DAS, showing reduced divergence (EMD) with preserved or improved interchange intervention accuracy, plus a modified causal-subspace CL loss with OOD gains in synthetic settings and an EMD-IIA regression analysis
Clear writing, good figures, detailed appendix (methodology, hyperparameters, additional divergence metrics), honest limitations section, and transparent LLM-usage statement
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the observation that activation patching takes representations off-manifold is known (acknowledged via Zhang & Nanda 2024, Stutz et al. 2019, Makelov et al. 2023), and the theoretical results are relatively simple — the circular-manifold proposition is essentially a coordinate-wise construction, and the patch-closure theorem is a short exercise; the core mitigation is an existing loss from Grant (2025) applied to an existing setting

The empirical divergence demonstration is largely qualitative (2D PCA plots) with ad hoc layer selection (layer 10 chosen for lowest EMD, layer 25 for SAE availability), and the paper correctly but weakly notes divergence presence does not establish any claims are wrong

The central practical claim — that minimizing divergence mitigates pernicious divergence — is not demonstrated on real models: hidden-pathway activation and dormant behavioral changes are shown only in small hand-constructed examples; the LLM experiment only shows reduced EMD with maintained IIA, and OOD benefits appear only on a simple 10-class synthetic dataset (30 trainings) where the EMD-IIA anti-correlation may be confounded

The proposed harm-classification framework (Algorithm 1) is approximate, unvalidated, and the authors concede that no principled method for classifying harmful divergence for a given claim is provided, leaving the paper more of a cautionary/position contribution than a solution

Significance is somewhat narrowed by the self-acknowledged scope limits: the modified CL loss is confined to synthetic settings, and the overall contribution is an 'initial step' whose actionable guidance for practitioners (e.g., when to trust patching results on real models) remains limited

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and under-examined question in mechanistic interpretability: whether causal interventions create off-distribution representations and what this means for the validity of patching-based conclusions.

The taxonomy of 'harmless' vs 'pernicious' divergence (null-space deviations vs hidden-pathway/dormant-behavior activation) is a useful conceptual framing, and the paper is commendably careful in stressing that harm is claim-dependent and that the categories are not mutually exclusive.

The paper combines theory, hand-constructed toy circuits (ReLU hidden-pathway example, dormant behavioral change example), and empirical measurements (EMD and other manifold metrics) across three popular intervention families (mean-difference patching, SAEs, Boundless DAS).

The toy examples in Section 4.2 are concrete and convincing demonstrations that behaviorally 'successful' interventions can recruit circuits that are silent under the natural distribution, which is a cautionary result for practitioners.

Honest limitation discussion: the authors acknowledge the modified CL loss is confined to narrow synthetic settings and that minimizing divergence magnitude does not guarantee elimination of hidden pathways.
The appendix provides substantial methodological detail (divergence metrics, dataset construction, hyperparameter sweeps), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions are largely trivial. Proposition 3.1 (a patched point on a circular manifold exceeds the class radius when both coordinates are patched at boundary values) is a two-line geometric observation, and the Appendix A.2 theorem (patch-closure characterizes Cartesian products) is straightforward. Neither requires the formal apparatus presented, and neither is surprising.

The central phenomenon — that off-manifold interventions can activate off-distribution circuits and yield misleading mechanistic conclusions — is already well known in the community through causal scrubbing, adversarial on-/off-manifold attack literature (Stutz et al., 2019), and subspace-patching illusions (Makelov et al., 2023). The paper's own related work section concedes this, weakening the novelty claim of contributions 1-3.

The proposed mitigation is incremental: the primary tool (Counterfactual Latent loss) is borrowed directly from Grant (2025) and merely applied to Boundless DAS; the 'modified' CL loss is a per-subspace variant of an existing objective. The methodological novelty is thin.

Empirical validation of the mitigation is very narrow. The LLM experiment only shows that divergence decreases while IIA is maintained — it does not demonstrate the claimed downstream benefit (improved OOD intervention accuracy), which is only shown on an 18-dimensional synthetic MLP task that is far removed from realistic interpretability settings.

The layer selection for the mean-difference experiments is post-hoc (layer 10 chosen because it had the lowest EMD of all layers), which risks biasing the divergence measurements; the paper notes this but does not adequately address the concern.

The claimed link between divergence and OOD performance rests on a linear regression with n=30 observations from the authors' own synthetic trainings; this is weak statistical evidence for a central hypothesis, and correlation between EMD and IIA may be confounded by training convergence.

The 'harmless vs pernicious' formalization does not yield an operational procedure for real models — the proposed Algorithm 1 is acknowledged by the authors to be an approximation that fails precisely in the pernicious cases the paper is most concerned about (dormant behavioral changes). Thus the practical payoff of the theory is limited.

No comparison against the most obvious alternative mitigation (projecting interventions onto the natural manifold/local PCA subspace, e.g., Veraart et al. 2024, which the paper itself cites), so it is unclear whether the CL loss approach is actually preferable to simpler baselines.

Some hyperparameter sweep results (Figures 6-9) appear inconsistent with the headline claim that CL loss improves OOD performance (e.g., at higher learning rates DAS+CL can underperform the behavioral-loss-only baseline), and the paper does not discuss when the mitigation fails.

Overall, the paper reads as a position/discussion paper with simple proofs, illustrative toy examples, and a narrow empirical study; the contribution does not rise to the level of a strong technical result or a broadly validated method for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question for mechanistic interpretability: whether causal interventions (activation patching, SAE reconstruction, DAS) move representations off the model's natural distribution, and whether that undermines the validity of downstream mechanistic claims.

Nice conceptual taxonomy distinguishing 'harmless' divergence (within behavioral null-spaces) from 'pernicious' divergence (activating hidden pathways or causing dormant behavioral changes), with the useful observation that harm is claim-dependent rather than intrinsic.

Combines theory and empirics: a simple but clean proof that coordinate patching guarantees off-manifold states for all manifold geometries except axis-aligned hyper-rectangles (Appendix A.2), hand-crafted worked examples of hidden-pathway activation (Sec. 4.2), and empirical demonstration of divergence across three real intervention methods on LLaMA models using EMD plus several additional off-manifold metrics in the appendix.

An attempt at mitigation: applying and modifying the Counterfactual Latent loss from Grant (2025) to Boundless DAS, with a hyperparameter sweep showing reduced divergence at preserved IIA, and a correlation between training EMD and OOD interchange intervention accuracy.
Honest about limitations (no principled perniciousness classifier, mitigation confined to simple settings) and transparent about LLM usage and code availability.
weaknesses: The central empirical observation — that interventions move representations off the natural manifold — is fairly intuitive and largely anticipated by prior work (noise-based patching, causal scrubbing, Makelov et al.'s subspace illusion); the paper itself acknowledges these precedents, which weakens the novelty of contribution 1.

The 'pernicious' cases, arguably the most important contribution, are demonstrated only in tiny hand-constructed two-layer circuits (Sec. 4.2) and a contrived balanced-subspace example (A.2.1). No evidence is provided that pernicious divergence actually occurs in real language models, so the practical significance of the taxonomy for real interpretability work remains untested.

The mitigation is incomplete and evaluated narrowly: CL loss is validated on a Boundless DAS tutorial notebook and small synthetic MLP tasks only; there is no demonstration on a genuinely challenging setting, and the modified CL loss targets causal dimensions only while the paper's own analysis says pernicious harm comes from null-space/dormant directions that the loss does not classify or control.
Algorithm 1 for classifying divergence as harmless vs. harmful is proposed but never evaluated, leaving a key gap between the diagnosis (Sec. 4) and the proposed remedy (Sec. 5).

Statistical support is thin in places: the EMD-vs-baseline comparison (Fig. 2c) uses few conditions, one layer per method, and the regression in A.6 has only 30 observations from a single synthetic task; the selection of layer 10 for MDVP because it had the lowest EMD introduces a potentially confounding choice.

Overall the paper positions itself as an 'initial step', and the evaluation matches that framing: the claimed advance (reliable interventions) is not yet demonstrated at a scale or difficulty where it would change practice for interpretability researchers.
